Right, everybody, Figure 3, and before anybody says what it means, I want you to tell me what it shows. On the horizontal axis we have days, from zero to fourteen. On the vertical axis, the percentage of seeds that germinated. Two groups. The black line is the control, the green line is the seeds we soaked overnight. Look at the green line first. Almost nothing happens for three days, then it rises sharply between day three and day six, from about ten percent to about sixty. After that the rise slows down, and it levels off at roughly eighty-five percent by day ten. The control rises too, but steadily, without that jump, and it finishes at about forty. So by the end, the soaked group is roughly twice as high as the control. There is one strange point, day eight in the control, where it suddenly drops to twenty and then comes back. That is one tray, and I would not build an argument on it. Notice what I have not said. I have not said why the soaking works. That is a different conversation, and it comes after this one.

Hi, it is me again. I have finished the table for the results section and I want to read it to you before I send it, because I am not sure the numbers say what I think they say. So, three sites, and we counted the same species at each one in March and again in August. At the first site, the number fell slightly, from forty-two to thirty-eight, which is honestly almost nothing. At the second site, it fell sharply, from fifty-five to nineteen, so it lost roughly two thirds. And at the third site it actually rose, from twelve to thirty, which is more than double. My problem is the summary sentence. I had written that the population declined across all sites, and that is just not true, is it? Two out of three declined, and the decline at the first site is so small it might be noise. I think the honest sentence is that it fell sharply at one site, barely changed at another, and more than doubled at the third. Can you tell me if that sounds too complicated for a results section?
